ambiguities.phrase: There are also derived results; each is completely fixed by the inputs given here, but its verified outcome has not been obtained yet.  ...versus...  At this point it has been established that neither K3 nor K4 holds and that K5 and K1 hold.
readings: The specific list of established values overrides the generic header: K3, K4, K5, K1 already have known (verified) values and are part of the decision state as given. This is the reading used in 'state' and the more plausible one.

The header is literal: no computed fact has a verified/certified outcome yet, so the listed value(s) of K3, K4, K5, K1 come from some unverified route; because the closing paragraph says a computed fact enters the decision state only through its verified result, they would not count until the matching computation is run. The text also offers a computation for an already-listed handle (RUN_SOLVER_K3, COMPUTE_POSTERIOR_K5, RUN_PRIMALITY_TEST_K1), which makes this reading less far-fetched.

awkward: Negation in front of a parenthesised group that is followed by an 'exactly/precisely when' can be attached either to the group alone or to the whole biconditional. The two parses are logically equivalent here (not(A iff B) is the same as (not A) iff B), so the formal content is not affected, but the same sentence shape with 'and'/'or' would be a real ambiguity. Phrase: '((it is not the case that (F2 does not hold) exactly when K6 holds) exactly when F1 does not hold)'.
Double negation written out instead of the plain handle: 'it is not the case that (F2 does not hold)'.
'K2 holds whenever K3 holds' and 'F1 holds whenever K4 does not hold' put the consequent first; unambiguous but easy to flip when skimming.

'Whenever F1 holds, F2 does not hold' and 'In every case where F2 holds, F1 does not hold' are the same constraint stated twice (contrapositives); harmless but may make a reader look for a difference.
